Learning Objectives
Describe common psychiatric conditions for the upper extremity.
Discuss potential presentations of psychiatric conditions.
Identify treatment strategies for psychiatric conditions.
Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders
Overview
Psychiatric disorders of the upper extremity are characterized by symptoms and incapability
out of proportion with that expected to result from the objective pathology.
The disorders are difficult to identify, may be a challenge to manage, and may place a
considerable burden on the medical field. A multidisciplinary approach via a combination of
medical and psychiatric interventions is critical for diagnosis and long-term management.



These disorders often are called nonorganic disorders because they often have no medical
origin; however, persistent simulation of disease, such as repetitive, self-induced hand swelling
observed in patients with Secretan disease, may lead to permanent dysfunction.

Overview
In identifying the etiology, surgeons must attempt to delineate conscious versus
unconscious motives, intentional production of symptoms and signs, and the presence
of external incentives. . This lesson reviews psychiatric illnesses with manifestations in
the hand and wrist. Psychiatric diagnoses are classified according the Diagnostic and
Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, which currently is in the 5th edition (DSM-5).1 1 In
prior editions, psychiatric illnesses with largely somatic manifestations were broadly
classified as somatoform, factitious, or malingering disorders. In the DSM-5, somatoform
and factitious disorders are defined under the umbrella of somatic symptoms and
related disorders. Malingering is no longer considered a medical or psychological
diagnosis.
Somatic Symptom Disorders of the Upper Extremity
In the DSM-5, a somatic symptom disorder (SSD) is characterized as one or more somatic
symptoms that are distressing or result in notable disruption of daily life, as well as excessive
and disproportionate thoughts, feelings, and behaviors regarding those symptoms.1

Somatic Symptom Disorders of the Upper Extremity
The individual must be persistently symptomatic for at least 6 months to be diagnosed
with SSD. One key change from prior editions is that a diagnosis of SSD no longer
requires that the somatic symptoms be medically unexplained. This change means that
the presenting symptoms may or may not be associated with another medical condition.
Parallels are drawn between this condition and depression, in the sense that it can occur
in the context of a serious medical condition.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Psychiatric Hand Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002068
2/15

Most often, a patient with SSD is unconsciously producing or embellishing physical
symptoms because of some underlying psychiatric factors. These symptoms may be
interpreted as indicative of a disease state but they cannot be understood in terms of
objective, measurable pathophysiology.
In the upper extremity, the most common presentations of SSD are conversion disorder,
clenched fist syndrome, and hypochondriasis.
Conversion Disorder/Functional Neurologic Symptom Disorder
In the DSM-5, conversion disorder was renamed as functional neurologic symptom disorder.1
Functional neurologic symptom disorder is diagnosed if an individual experiences neurologic
symptoms inconsistent with a neurologic disease, but the symptoms are genuine and cause
distress and/or impairment.
Criteria for diagnosis include the following:
One or more transient symptoms that affect voluntary motor or sensory function are
present or cause transient loss of consciousness.
After appropriate medical assessment, a very low probability exists that the symptom is the
result of a general medical condition, the direct effect of a substance, or a culturally
sanctioned behavior or experience.
One or more diagnostic factors provide evidence of internal inconsistency or incongruity
with known pathologies.
The symptom causes substantial distress or incapacity in social, occupational, or other
important areas of functioning or the individual continues to seek medical evaluation.
In the upper extremity, symptoms may include any of the following:
Resting tremor or abnormal motion (psychogenic nonepileptic seizures)
Weakness or paralysis
Loss of sensation or atypical sensory symptoms
Unusual posturing or dystonia (hyperflexed, hyperextended, or clenched hand)
The onset of symptoms frequently is associated with trauma or a postoperative state.

Conversion Disorder/Functional Neurologic Symptom Disorder

Although a psychologic or traumatic stressor often is present, it is not a requirement to
establish the diagnosis. Risk factors include a diagnosis of a mental health or neurologic
disorder, family history of a functional neurologic symptom disorder, history of physical
or sexual abuse or psychological trauma, and female sex (2 to 3 times higher in females
compared with males).2
Clenched Fist
Clenched fist, also known as psychoflexed hand, is the condition in which an individual keeps
at least one finger on one or both hands tightly clenched (Figure 1).
Figure 1 Dorsal (A) and palmar (B) view clinical photographs of a clenched right hand show a
flexion contracture in the metacarpal and interphalangeal joints. (Reproduced from Birman
MV, Lee DH: Factitious disorders of the upper extremity. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2012;20[2]:78-
85.) 

Clenched Fist
Initially described in hand surgery journals in 1980 by Simmons and Vasile,3 flexion is
more commonly noted in the ulnar three digits. Early on in the syndrome, passive
motion can be attained via distraction or anesthesia. With progression, joint flexion
contractures, tendon adhesions, and skin maceration or pressure wounds because of
nail impingement in the palm may occur.
Psychogenic clenched fist should be differentiated from neurogenic clenched fist.
Psychogenic clenched fist is associated with a psychologic origin and is theorized to often
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Psychiatric Hand Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002068
4/15

result from an ego protective mechanism by which the hand(s) are clenched, protecting
the individual from acting on a psychologically unacceptable impulse or thought.3
Neurogenic clenched fist may occur in the setting of unmasking primitive grasp reflexes
in patients suffering from central neurologic disorders, such as Parkinson or Alzheimer
disease. In addition, neurogenic clenched fist may be a manifestation of spasticity after a
cerebrovascular accident.
Hypochondriasis
Hypochondriasis is described as a fixation on benign symptoms as a premonition of a more
serious illness.
The preoccupation persists despite adequate medical evaluation and reassurance.
The fixation causes substantial distress or impairment and may inhibit social functioning.

Hypochondriasis
A diagnosis requires a duration of more than 6 months and exclusion of specific
pathology or mental illness. According to new criteria in the DSM-5, radiographic-
confirmed mild osteoarthritis or electrodiagnostically mild median neuropathy at the
carpal tunnel associated with substantial intense and disruptive symptoms and activity
intolerance for more than 6 months is considered an SSD.
Diagnosis and Management
Management of SSD benefits from coordination between disciplines.
The surgeon’s role is to gain the trust of the patient to limit tests and treatment, particularly
surgical treatment.
Surgical treatment is avoided, even if superimposed medical pathology (eg, wounds, stiffness)
is present, until the underlying mental health issue is addressed.
Often, individuals with SSD have difficulty understanding that their somatic representation of
illness is a manifestation of an underlying psychiatric condition. The surgeon can coordinate
with the patient’s other clinicians.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Psychiatric Hand Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002068
5/15

Their combined expertise and relationship with the patient may, with time and gentle nudging,
generate insight.

Diagnosis and Management
Effort-related weakness may have a collapsing or give way quality that is not associated
with true motor nerve pathology. Mental health–related tremors, which also are known
as psychogenic tremors, can be halted temporarily via externally paced tapping
movements of the contralateral limb or other distraction techniques. Nerve conduction
studies can detect important neuropathology but should only be ordered in patients
with relatively high pre-test odds that measurable pathophysiology can account for
some or all of the symptoms and in whom a test result would lead to an important
treatment option. Testing in a low probability setting is associated with notable potential
harms from undue emphasis on and over-management of incidental, and likely
asymptomatic, concomitant pathology, such as mild median neuropathy at the carpal
tunnel. A neurology consultation may be helpful if a neurological condition unfamiliar to
an orthopaedic surgeon or hand specialist may be causing symptoms. If patients
demonstrate insight into the relationship between mental and physical health, they may
be open to meeting with a psychologist or psychiatrist. Surgeons should show
compassion; be supportive; avoid tests, diagnoses, and treatment options with greater
potential for harm than benefit; and set up a collaboration by informing the patient’s
regular clinicians about the potential mental health opportunity.
Factitious Disorders of the Upper Extremity
A factitious disorder is defined as the purposeful or intentional production of disease to relieve
emotional distress.1 An individual creates or worsens pathophysiology intentionally.
Dissimilar from SSD, disease production itself is a conscious behavior; however, the underlying
motivation is unconscious. In prior DSM editions, the motivation was attributed to the
individual’s internal incentive to assume a sick role.
The DSM-5 notes that the deceptive behavior is evident in the absence of external incentives.
Patients with a factitious disorder often have multiple care clinicians, hospital admissions, and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Psychiatric Hand Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002068
6/15

may undergo numerous invasive and/or surgical procedures.
The prevalence is difficult to determine because of the secretive nature of the disorder.

Factitious Disorders of the Upper Extremity
Factitious disorders are now classified as factitious disorder imposed on self (FDIS) and
factitious disorder imposed on another (FDIA) and range from mild to severe. A factitious
disorder previously was referred to as Munchausen syndrome. Certain studies retain the
eponym to refer to the most severe or chronic cases of FDIS (Munchausen syndrome)
and FDIA (Munchausen-by-proxy). Dissimilar from SSD, in which unconscious production
or embellishing of symptoms occurs, FDIS is consciously motivated. Individuals with FDIS
feign illness or injury not for a specific gain but to gain sympathy and attention similar to
that given to individuals who are truly ill. FDIS is notable for self-induced infections, self-
induced injuries, and simulation of clinical manifestation of various diseases. Patients
often are willing to undergo painful tests or surgical procedures to attain recognition and
attention from others. A factitious disorder is quite distinct from the somatic expression
of mental illness characteristic of SSD. In the upper extremity, FDIS is classified by clinical
problem and syndrome.
Factitious Dermatitis
Factitious dermatitis, also known as dermatitis artifacta, is a condition in which skin lesions are
inflicted by the patient's own actions without any rational motivation for the behavior (Figure
2).

7/15

Figure 2 Clinical photographs of the dorsum of bilateral forearms show multiple, well-
demarcated, linear, longitudinal erosions, all of which are characteristic of factitious
dermatitis. (Reproduced with permission from Varyani N, Garg S, Gupta G, Singh S, Tripathi K:
Trichotillomania and dermatitis artefacta: A rare coexistence. Case Rep Psychiatry
2012;2012:674136.)

Factitious Dermatitis
They typically are observed only on the accessible portions of the body. In the hand, this
often manifests as a nonhealing ulcer or a postoperative wound dehiscence. Wounds
can be created or made less healthy via subcutaneous or intravenous introduction of
foreign materials, leading to cellulitis, abscesses, or septicemia.
Factitious Lymphedema
Factitious lymphedema results from the intentional application of tourniquets or constrictive
devices to the arm, repetitive intentional blows to the upper extremity, or repetitive irritation
of the skin (Figure 3).
Careful physical examination of the entire limb is required to assess for lesions or distinctive
circumferential indurations that may be indicative of self-inflicted constriction.4SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Psychiatric Hand Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002068
8/15

A broken window-pane pattern of lymphedema often is observed distal to the constriction.
Secretan disease is a type of factitious lymphedema caused by repetitive blows to the dorsum
of the hand, resulting in dorsal peritendinous fibrosis.5
Figure 3 Clinical photograph of the left upper extremity of a 20-year-old woman shows
lymphedema. The orthopaedic team was consulted for amputation of the extremity. No injury
was documented, and no underlying pathology was observed on MRIs, vascular Doppler
ultrasonographic images, or laboratory studies. The patient exhibited characteristic factitious

AAOS | Psychiatric Hand Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002068
9/15

behavior; a Velcro strap was found on the upper arm during morning rounds, and the patient
became angry when confronted. The patient underwent below-elbow amputation in a Caribbean
country. (Courtesy of Robert J. Strauch, MD, New York, NY.)

Factitious Lymphedema
Typically, elevation and/or serial cast immobilization will resolve the edema. The role of
the physician is to exclude medical causes of lymphedema and coordinate care with the
patient’s other clinicians to encourage appropriate mental health care and limit
iatrogenic harm from tests, diagnoses, and procedures.
Factitious Subcutaneous Lymphedema

Factitious Subcutaneous Lymphedema
Subcutaneous, self-inflicted injection of air into the soft tissues of the upper extremity
has been reported.6 Imaging studies may increase concern for gas gangrene or
necrotizing fasciitis; however, the clinical presentation and laboratory workup does not
correspond with infection7 (Resource 1).
Munchausen Syndrome
Individuals with Munchausen syndrome frequently seek medical attention and may present
with drastic symptoms; however, no underlying pathology is identified.

Munchausen Syndrome
Frequently, individuals have undergone an extensive workup, have extensive knowledge
of medical terminology and disease pathology, and have failed the traditional therapies
for the said disease or diagnosis. An in-depth assessment often will reveal multiple
medical clinicians and frequent hospitalizations without a formal diagnosis. Individuals
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Psychiatric Hand Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002068
10/15

may be eager to undergo invasive procedures or tests. Disease manifestations
eventually are discovered to be self-inflicted. The psychologic gain is attention or
achieving the sick role in contrast to malingering, in which the secondary gain is clear (eg,
avoiding work by simulating illness). Munchausen syndrome by proxy occurs if
symptoms or manifestations are intentionally manufactured by another individual;
children are especially vulnerable to experiencing this by an adult caregiver.
Diagnosis and Management
Diagnostic and treatment strategies are similar to those for SSDs. If appropriate, additional
information from family or friends may be helpful; however, specialists generally should leave
these inquiries to a trusted regular clinician, such as a primary care physician.
Diagnosis of a factitious disorder requires falsified symptoms and evidence of factitious
behavior (ie, direct observation of self-infliction, tampering with records or laboratory test
results). Clinical suspicion of factitious disorder is elevated with the following:8
Use of multiple healthcare facilities
High rates of hospitalizations or clinician visits
Refusal to grant access to information from external sources
Numerous drug allergies
Few visitors
Inconsistent patient histories and symptoms
Willingness to undergo invasive procedures
Opposition to psychiatric evaluation (does not exclude factitious disorder)
Disruptive behavior
Unusual illness course
Worsening of symptoms immediately before planned discharge

Diagnosis and Management
Management usually is a combination of medical and psychiatric treatment options.
Tests should be limited to only those deemed essential. Similar to SSD, successful
management depends on a trusting relationship and insight into the role of mental
health in the illness. Hand surgeons and orthopaedic surgeons have fulfilled their role if
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Psychiatric Hand Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002068
11/15

they avoid unhelpful tests, diagnoses, and management and coordinate with the
patient’s primary caregivers.
Malingering
Malingering is not considered a formal medical or psychiatric diagnosis. Malingering is
intentionally feigning or exaggerating illness because of some external motivation. The reason
for this deception is tangible and rationally understandable. Malingering often is observed in
individuals attempting to avoid requirements, such military duty or work; obtain financial
compensation, evade criminal prosecution, or obtain drugs. This is in contrast to
Muchenhausen syndrome, in which assumption of the sick role and attention is the
motivation. The DSM-5 notes that malingering should be suspected in the presence of the
following:1
Medicolegal presentation (eg, an attorney refers the patient; a patient is seeking
compensation for an alleged injury)
Marked discrepancy between the intensity of symptoms and the magnitude of activity
intolerance and the objective pathophysiology
Lack of cooperation during evaluation and limited adherence to prescribed management
Presence of an antisocial personality disorde

Malingering
On clinical examination, individuals with malingering rarely have objective findings. The
individual may attempt to create objective findings by manipulating the physical
examination, such as with limited effort with strength testing or with resistance to
passive motion. Diagnostic tips for clinicians include prolonged and repeated physical
examination performed to attempt to fatigue the patient and assess for inconsistent
responses. Neuromuscular deficits often do to not follow known anatomic distribution.
The clinician must document all tests to identify discrepancies over time.
Conclusion
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:55 PM
AAOS | Psychiatric Hand Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002068
12/15

Mental health is a part of every illness. The named and discrete psychiatric hand disorders are
just the extreme presentations of everyday aspects of human illness behavior.
Surgeons can attend to these diagnoses as carefully as they attend to the diagnosis of
musculoskeletal pathophysiology. Accurate diagnosis of mental (eg, distress, misconceptions)
and social (eg, malingering, also known as secondary gain) health opportunities is important to
avoid iatrogenic harm from potentially erroneous diagnoses and low value and potentially
harmful tests, diagnoses, and treatment options.
Coordination with other clinicians is the most important aspect of treatment if mental health is
an important component of the illness.
